entries.label: Width of the band around a size threshold in which businesses count as near it
entries.units: share of the threshold on either side (0.1 = ±10%)

citation.title: Forward plan: prospective policy costing in ALICIA

entries.quote: Screen: count firms within ±10% of the threshold (CABEE size bands; turnover bands from ATO).
entries.derivation: The plan's screening band, ±10% of the threshold. Fixed: it defines the screen, it is not an estimate.
entries.notes: The tool's assumption, graded D: no source sets the width of the band. CABEE size bands are coarse (0, 1–4, 5–19, 20–199, 200+ employees), so in practice the band is approximated by the size bands that overlap it.

entries.label: Upper bound: welfare cost of size-contingent labour regulation (France, 50 employees)

citation.authors: Luis Garicano, Claire Lelarge and John Van Reenen
citation.title: Firm Size Distortions and the Productivity Distribution: Evidence from France

entries.quote: In our baseline case with French levels of partial real wage inflexibility, welfare costs of the regulations are 3.4 percent of GDP (falling to 1.3 percent if real wages were perfectly flexible downward).
entries.derivation: Value = the paper's baseline (3.4% of GDP, French partial wage inflexibility); low = its flexible-wage case (1.3%). The paper reports nothing above the baseline, so high = value.
entries.notes: Read in the abstract only ([A]). A structural estimate for France, where many labour laws bind at 50 employees; it covers the whole set of rules at that threshold. F-C5-02 scales it by the share of employment near the threshold (A-P05).

entries.label: Tax equivalent of France's 50-employee regulations

citation.authors: Luis Garicano, Claire Lelarge and John Van Reenen
citation.title: Firm Size Distortions and the Productivity Distribution: Evidence from France

entries.quote: We find that the cost of these regulations is equivalent to that of a 2.3 percent variable tax on labor.
entries.derivation: Value = the abstract's tax equivalent (2.3%). Fixed: the abstract gives no range, and the uncertainty is carried by the welfare-cost bounds.
entries.notes: Lets a user compare their threshold's cost per worker with the French rules before scaling the bounds.

entries.label: Lower bound: output per worker gained by removing France's 50-employee regulations

citation.title: Size-Dependent Regulations, Firm Size Distribution, and Reallocation

entries.quote: Removing the regulation improves labor allocation across firms, leading in steady state to an increase in output per worker slightly less than 0.3%, holding the number of firms fixed. However, if firm entry is elastic, the steady-state gains are an order of magnitude smaller.
entries.derivation: Value = the abstract's figure with the number of firms fixed ("slightly less than 0.3%", taken as 0.3). Low = an order of magnitude smaller (0.03%) when entry is elastic.
entries.notes: Read in the abstract only ([A]). The abstract also says the regulation is equivalent to a sunk cost of "about 1 year of an average employee salary" plus a 0.04% payroll tax. Units differ from the upper bound (output per worker, not welfare as a share of GDP); F-C5-02 treats both as shares of output (A-P05).

entries.label: Check: change in the number of firms just below the SA payroll-tax threshold
entries.units: % change in the number of firms

citation.authors: Dan Andrews, Jack Buckley and Rachel Lee
citation.title: A counterproductive tax cut? How size-based payroll taxes can create a roadblock to firm growth

entries.quote: A large number of firms bunched just below the $1.5m threshold to avoid paying the higher marginal tax rate. The number of firms just below the threshold increased by 21%, while the number just above decreased by 18%.
entries.derivation: Value = the summary's figure (+21%). Fixed: a check on the C5 bounds, not an input to them; the note gives no interval.
entries.notes: An Australian check on F-C5-02 (traceability: E61-2024). The SA reform raised the marginal payroll-tax rate for payrolls between $1.5m and $1.7m from 4.95% to roughly 27% (p. 3).

entries.label: Check: change in the number of firms just above the SA payroll-tax threshold
entries.units: % change in the number of firms

citation.authors: Dan Andrews, Jack Buckley and Rachel Lee
citation.title: A counterproductive tax cut? How size-based payroll taxes can create a roadblock to firm growth

entries.quote: The number of firms just below the threshold increased by 21%, while the number just above decreased by 18%.
entries.derivation: Value = the summary's figure (−18%). Fixed: a check, not an input.

entries.label: Check: change in total payroll of firms just above the SA payroll-tax threshold

citation.authors: Dan Andrews, Jack Buckley and Rachel Lee
citation.title: A counterproductive tax cut? How size-based payroll taxes can create a roadblock to firm growth

entries.quote: We estimate that firms just above the threshold decreased their payrolls by $5.9m (3.3%), more than offsetting a $3.5m increase by smaller firms.
entries.derivation: Value = the summary's figure (−3.3%, −$5.9m). Fixed: a check, not an input.
entries.notes: From a bunching estimator (Saez 2010) of the elasticity of taxable payroll (p. 3). The authors say the estimates give "a general sense of the scale" and do not account for other factors.
